Yet, in the shadow of this sacred principle, a profound injustice festers. A stain on our nation’s soul. The systematic, purposeful disenfranchisement of our fellow citizens – simply because they have been convicted of a felony – is a betrayal of everything we claim to hold dear.

We gather not just to advocate, but to demand. We demand an end to this archaic, discriminatory practice that steals voices, silences communities, and perpetuates a cycle of marginalization. We stand here today to declare, with one thunderous voice: Restoring the vote to all citizens with felony convictions, including those currently incarcerated, is not just policy – it is justice. It is moral imperative. It is the only path to a truly universal suffrage worthy of the name.

Let’s be clear: The right to vote is the bedrock of citizenship. It is how we hold power accountable. It is how we shape our own destiny. It is how we say, "My life matters, my voice counts, my future is part of this nation’s future." To strip this right away – often permanently, often for non-violent offenses, often disproportionately targeting communities of color – is to declare that person less than human. Less than a citizen. It is a modern form of civic exile, a punishment that extends far beyond the sentence served, designed to permanently subjugate entire populations.

Look at the history. This didn’t happen by accident. This is the deliberate legacy of the 13th Amendment, with its insidious loophole: "Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude... except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted." From the Black Codes to Jim Crow, the disenfranchisement of Black Americans has been a cornerstone of systemic oppression. Today, felony disenfranchisement continues that brutal legacy. It is a tool of racial control. One in every 16 Black adults is barred from voting – a rate four times higher than that of white adults. This is not coincidence; this is continuation.

And let’s dismantle the cynical arguments, once and for all. "If you break the law, you lose your say"? Rubbish! Voting is not a reward for good behavior; it is the fundamental mechanism for changing behavior and laws. How can we expect rehabilitation, how can we expect reintegration into society, if we permanently brand someone as outside the political community? Stripping the vote doesn’t teach responsibility; it teaches resentment and exclusion. It tells a person, "You are forever an outsider."

We hear whispers of "public safety." Let me be unequivocal: There is no evidence that disenfranchisement enhances public safety. In fact, studies suggest the opposite. Restoring voting rights increases civic engagement, strengthens community ties, and fosters a sense of belonging – all proven deterrents to recidivism. And what about those behind bars? Being incarcerated does not erase your humanity. It does not erase your status as a citizen. It does not erase your stake in the laws that govern you, the policies that affect your family, the community you will one day rejoin. Friends, the fight for voting rights restoration is the fight for the soul of America. It is the fight against the systemic disenfranchisement that has plagued us since our founding. It is the fight to realize the promise of "We the People," not "We the Privileged."

This is not radical. This is democracy. This is justice. This is honoring the fundamental equality upon which this nation was supposedly built.

So I call upon every legislator listening: Tear down these barriers of prejudice and control. Pass laws that restore voting rights fully and immediately. I call upon every governor: Use your pen to erase the stain of civic exile. I call upon every citizen: Demand better. Register voters. Organize. Mobilize. The arc of the universe bends towards justice, but only if we bend it. Let us bend it here. Let us bend it now. Let us restore the vote to every citizen. Let us build a democracy where everyone has a seat at the table, where every voice is heard, and where the promise of universal suffrage is finally, fully realized.
